paragraphs.heading: What it was
paragraphs.text: The Holocaust, called the Shoah in Hebrew, was the genocide of Europe's Jews during World War II. Between 1941 and 1945, Nazi Germany and those who worked with it murdered around six million Jews. That was roughly two out of every three Jews in Europe. It is regarded as the deadliest single genocide in human history, and in Western memory it has come to stand for the worst evil people can do.

paragraphs.heading: The names
paragraphs.text: The English word holocaust comes from a Greek word for a burnt offering, and for centuries it simply meant destruction by fire or, more loosely, a massacre. In the 1950s it began to be used as a name for the Nazi killing of the Jews, and by the 1970s, written with a capital H, it was the standard term. The Hebrew word Shoah means catastrophic destruction and refers only to Jewish victims. The killers themselves hid what they were doing behind the phrase "Final Solution".

paragraphs.heading: Old hatreds, new theories
paragraphs.text: Jews had lived in Europe for more than two thousand years. In the Middle Ages they faced antisemitism, hostility toward Jews that rested on Christian teaching blaming them for the death of Jesus. In the 18th and 19th centuries a political form appeared, driven by rising nationalism and by industry that sharpened economic clashes between Jews and non-Jews; it spoke of a "Jewish question" and often of a worldwide Jewish plot. Some scientists sorted humans into races locked in a fight to the death, and many racists claimed that Jews were a separate race foreign to Europe.

paragraphs.heading: The Nazis in power
paragraphs.text: The Nazi Party was founded after World War I, and its ideology is often named as the main reason the Holocaust happened. The Nazis saw the German nation as a racial community not limited by the country's borders, and wanted to cleanse it of people they judged racially foreign. They also wanted Lebensraum, or living space, to colonise in Eastern Europe. After taking power in early 1933, they tried to force every German Jew to leave the country. They passed laws against Jews, encouraged violence against them, and in November 1938 organised a nationwide attack on Jews known as Kristallnacht.

paragraphs.heading: From ghettos to mass murder
paragraphs.text: Once Germany invaded Poland in September 1939, the occupiers started to set up ghettos to segregate Jews, keeping them apart from everyone else. After Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, German forces and local collaborators killed 1.5 to 2 million Jews. At first the killers aimed at Jewish Red Army prisoners and civilian men, but they soon moved on to women and children. By early 1942, after the Wannsee Conference chaired by Reinhard Heydrich, the Final Solution was in action: a plan to murder every Jew in Europe.

paragraphs.heading: The camps
paragraphs.text: Most killing was done by mass shootings in Eastern Europe and in gas chambers at extermination camps in occupied Poland, chiefly Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Belzec, Sobibor, Chełmno and Majdanek. People who survived the trip to an extermination camp were gassed. Others went to forced labour camps, where many died of hunger, abuse or exhaustion, or after being made subjects of experiments. The killing peaked during Operation Reinhard, from March 1942 to November 1943, and most victims died in 1942, yet the murders went on until 1945. The belongings of the dead were handed out to German occupiers and other non-Jews.

paragraphs.heading: Other victims
paragraphs.text: Nazi persecution at the same time killed millions of people who were not Jewish, both civilians and prisoners of war. The word Holocaust is sometimes stretched to cover other groups, especially the Roma and Sinti, Soviet prisoners of war, and Polish and Soviet civilians. Each of these groups, though, was targeted for its own reasons.

paragraphs.heading: Afterwards
paragraphs.text: After the war many Jewish survivors left Europe. Fairly few of the killers were ever put on trial. Billions of dollars have been paid in reparations, but this has not matched what Europe's Jews lost. The Holocaust is remembered today through museums, memorials and culture.
